back: Income too low to buy the basic necessities of life: food, clean water, shelter, clothing and basic healthcare.
Income well below the average of the society, often below 50% or 60% of median income.
Unemployment, low wages, illness, age, environmental factors (also lack of education, assets and credit).

front: Give three policies that raise the incomes of the poor.
back: Economic growth; education and training; healthcare; minimum wage; credit and training for small producers.

front: Give three ways to redistribute income.
back: Progressive taxes; transfer payments (grants, pensions); free or subsidised public services; lower taxes on necessities.
Not necessarily: if all incomes rise at the same rate, the median rises too and relative poverty is unchanged.

front: Why is VAT on basic foods regressive?
back: The poor spend almost all their income, much of it on food, so the tax takes a larger share of their income.

front: Limit of a minimum wage as an anti-poverty policy?
back: It does not cover informal workers or the unemployed, and if set too high it may reduce formal jobs.
The income level below which a person or household is counted as poor (absolute: cost of basic needs; relative: a fraction of median income).
